I can’t edit the image here. Below are clear, non‑destructive instructions you can follow in different tools to change a plain gray background to blue while leaving the person untouched.

Quick note before starting
- Make a backup copy of the original file.
- Work with layers and masks so you can undo or refine without altering the original pixels.

Photoshop (recommended)
1. Duplicate the Background layer (Layer > Duplicate Layer).
2. With the copy selected, choose Select > Subject. (If Select Subject misses hair, use the Quick Selection or Object Selection tool to add/subtract.)
3. Click Select and Mask… — use the Refine Edge Brush over hair and soft edges. Set Output To: Layer Mask and click OK.
4. Create a Solid Color fill layer (Layer > New Fill Layer > Solid Color) using your blue (e.g., #1E90FF or #007BFF). Place this fill layer below the masked layer so the subject shows over blue.
5. Tidy the mask: paint on the mask with a soft black/white brush to remove or restore background where needed. Use Shift Edge / Feather in Select and Mask for smoother edges.
6. Remove gray fringe: on the masked subject layer, Layer > Matting > Defringe (1–2 px) or use Select and Mask > Decontaminate Colors.
7. Preserve shadows (if present): duplicate the original background, place it above the blue layer but under the subject layer, desaturate and set blend mode to Multiply or Overlay and reduce opacity until the shadow looks natural.

GIMP
1. Duplicate the image layer.
2. Use Select > Foreground Select or the Paths tool to isolate the person. Refine selection around hair manually if needed.
3. With the selection active, add a Layer Mask to the duplicated layer and initialize from selection.
4. Add a new layer below and fill it with your blue (#1E90FF or similar).
5. Paint on the layer mask (black to hide, white to reveal) to refine edges.
6. To remove fringe: select the mask and use Filters > Blur > Gaussian Blur (very small radius) then manually paint corrections; or shrink the selection by 1–2 px and reapply to reduce halo.
7. For shadows, duplicate the original background, desaturate and use Multiply mode above the blue layer but below the subject.

ImageMagick (command‑line; works well because background is uniform gray)
- If the gray is uniform and reasonably different from the subject, use a fuzz chroma-key approach:
  1) convert input.png -fuzz 12% -transparent "#808080" transparent.png
     (replace "#808080" with the exact gray hex if known; adjust -fuzz from ~5–20% depending on anti‑aliasing)
  2) convert -size WxH xc:"#1E90FF" blue.png   (replace WxH with image width and height or create from input)
  3) convert blue.png transparent.png -compose over -composite result.png
- If you need to preserve shadows that are grayish, you may need a more careful mask (manual mask creation in an editor) because pure thresholding can remove subtle background shadows.

Mobile / quick apps
- Use a background-erase tool that creates a mask (e.g., “Background Eraser”, “Remove.bg” (web), or advanced phone editors). Export with transparent background, then open in an editor and place a blue fill layer underneath. In apps without layers, prefer ones that let you refine the selection and keep soft transition options.

Edge / quality tips
- Hair and fine edges: use a refine-edge brush (Photoshop Select and Mask or manual smudging in GIMP). Decontaminate color to remove gray spill.
- Halos: shrink the mask by 1–2 px if a gray halo remains, then feather 0.5–1 px for smoothness.
- Color match: pick a blue that complements skin tones; dodge/burn or small color adjustments on the subject layer are okay but avoid recoloring the person if you must "leave the person untouched."
- Shadows: to keep natural contact shadows, recreate them as a semi‑transparent dark copy of the original background placed between subject and blue background with Multiply and lowered opacity.
- Output: Save layered file (PSD/XCF) and export flattened PNG/JPEG for sharing.

Suggested blue hexes
- Dodger Blue: #1E90FF
- Web/Primary Blue: #007BFF
- Deep Blue: #0057D9

If you tell me which tool you’ll use (Photoshop, GIMP, ImageMagick, or a phone app) and can give the exact gray hex (or attach the file elsewhere), I’ll give a tailored step‑by‑step with precise settings (fuzz %, px values, layer order, etc.).
